client: I just don’t know how to feel normal anymore. Ever since my dad died two months ago, everything feels gray and pointless. My friends keep inviting me out, but I don’t even have the energy to text them back—and when I do go, I just feel like I’m pretending to be okay.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of heaviness since your dad passed, and it’s understandable that things feel gray and draining right now. When you say you’re “pretending to be okay” around friends, I wonder if you feel like you *should* be moving on or showing up differently than you are. Would you say that’s true?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, that's exactly it. I feel like everyone expects me to be over it by now, but I'm not. It's been six months and I still cry in the shower most mornings. When I'm with friends, I force myself to laugh at their jokes, but it just makes me feel more alone because they don't know how broken I still feel inside. 

Sometimes I wonder if there's something wrong with me that I'm not "getting better" as fast as other people seem to. My sister seems to be handling it so much better than I am.
therapist: It sounds like you’re holding a lot of pressure to meet others’ expectations while carrying this deep grief—and that comparison to your sister adds another layer of pain. When you describe forcing laughter while feeling broken inside, I hear how exhausting that must be. Grief doesn’t follow a timeline—would it feel different if you let yourself honor your own pace?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I know logically that grief doesn't have a timeline, but it's hard when everyone else seems to think I should be "over it" by now. My sister was always the strong one, and I feel like I'm disappointing everyone by still struggling so much. The worst part is pretending I'm okay - it makes me feel even more alone.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying not just your grief, but also the weight of others' expectations—and that double burden must feel so isolating. When you talk about your sister being "the strong one," I wonder if part of your pain comes from feeling like your way of grieving isn't valid? That loneliness seems even heavier when you're pretending for others' comfort.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
Yeah, that hits hard. I do feel like I have to put on a brave face around my family because they keep saying how strong my sister is handling everything. It makes me feel like my sadness is just...too much for them. Like I'm failing at grieving "correctly" or something. 

Sometimes I think they'd rather I just pretend to be okay like she does. But when I'm alone, it all crashes down and I feel even more isolated because no one sees how much I'm really struggling.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two painful places—feeling pressured to perform strength for your family, then left alone with the full weight of your sadness. That line about "failing at grieving correctly" really stands out—what would grieving "your way" look like, if you didn't have to consider anyone else's expectations?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if I even remember how to grieve my way anymore. Everyone keeps telling me to be strong for my mom and siblings, but when I'm alone at night, it all hits me so hard that I can't breathe. The idea of grieving "my way" just makes me feel guilty—like I'd be selfish for falling apart when they need me.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying not just your own grief, but also the worry of letting others down—and that’s an incredibly heavy load. When you talk about those moments alone at night, I hear how overwhelming it feels, and I wonder if part of the guilt comes from feeling like you can’t fully honor your own pain while supporting your family. How does that tension sit with you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It’s hard to describe, but it feels like I’m being pulled in two directions. On one hand, I’m grieving and just want to let myself feel it, but on the other, I feel like I have to be strong for everyone else. It’s exhausting, and sometimes I wonder if I’m even doing either of them right. I feel guilty for wanting to focus on my own pain because it feels selfish, but I also feel like I’m failing my family by not being there for them enough.
therapist: You're describing such a painful tug-of-war—between honoring your grief and meeting your family's needs—and I hear how drained that leaves you. The way your voice softens when you talk about guilt makes me wonder if part of you has started believing you don’t *deserve* to prioritize your own pain? That burden of “doing it right” sounds especially heavy—what would happen if you let that expectation go, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know if I *can* let that expectation go. Every time I try to take time for myself, I hear my mom's voice in my head saying "we all have to make sacrifices." It's like if I'm not constantly holding everything together, I'm failing them. But you're right—I am so tired. 

The idea that I might deserve to prioritize my own pain feels... uncomfortable. Like I'd be selfish or weak for doing that. But I also can't keep going like this.
therapist: That voice of your mom’s—the one about sacrifices—seems to have become a kind of internal rulebook, and I hear how tightly it’s holding you. When you say the idea of prioritizing your pain feels uncomfortable, I wonder if that’s because you’ve been treating your grief like something to be managed rather than felt? You’re naming such an important tension: the exhaustion of holding everything up while fearing you’ll collapse under it. What would it feel like to set that burden down, even briefly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It’s hard to even imagine setting that burden down. If I do, it feels like I’m betraying everything my mom taught me—like I’m being selfish or ungrateful. I’ve carried this guilt for so long that it feels like part of who I am. Letting go, even briefly, sounds terrifying because what if I can’t pick it back up? What if I fall apart completely?
therapist: It sounds like this guilt has become so deeply tied to your sense of self that the idea of letting it go feels almost like losing a part of who you are. That fear of falling apart completely—what do you imagine would happen if you did? Sometimes, the things we’re most afraid of holding are also the things we most need to let ourselves feel.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I’ve never thought about it that way, but you’re right—it does feel like letting go of the guilt would leave me empty or incomplete. I guess I’m scared that if I stop beating myself up, I’ll just become careless or selfish. It’s like I’ve built my whole identity around being the person who’s always fixing things or making up for mistakes. Without that, who would I even be?
therapist: It sounds like you're realizing how much of your identity has been shaped by this role of being the one who fixes things—and that realization seems to bring both relief and fear. When you talk about becoming "careless or selfish," I hear how protective that guilt has felt, like it’s been keeping you from something worse. What do you think that fear might be trying to keep safe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I never thought about it that way before—that the guilt might actually be protecting me from something. I guess if I stop feeling guilty about not fixing everything, then... what? Maybe people won't need me anymore? That's scary because being needed is how I know I matter. But at the same time, always being the fixer is exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to notice how deeply tied your sense of worth is to being needed—and how exhausting that role can be. That idea of stepping away from always fixing things seems to bring up both fear and possibility—what might it feel like to matter simply for *who you are*, not just for what you do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
